title: Strip out AI stocks, and the US market lags Europe
source_used: Yahoo Finance (reporter Jake Conley); read in full via fulltext
key_facts: The S&P 500 is up roughly 13.5% since the start of the year, adding about $9 trillion in market value, lifted by tech.
An index of the so-called "old economy" that removes AI-related names has gained 5.5% since 1 Jan, against roughly 5.6% for Europe's STOXX 600.
BNP Paribas economists James Egelhof and Andrew Husby wrote that the bloc has probably missed out on the AI investment boom.

The article says AI did not create the US advantage but is magnifying it: the US and Canada account for about 60% of new data-centre capacity in 2026 against about 10% for Europe (Goldman Sachs); the eurozone hosts 5% of computing capacity against about three-quarters in the US (ECB).
Goldman Sachs says AI investment adds only about 0.1 percentage point to European GDP growth in 2026; euro-area third-quarter growth is tracking 0.2%.
US hyperscalers now account for roughly 10% of new euro bond issuance by non-financial firms (Apollo Global data).
Europe has advantages too: a free-cash-flow yield of about 5.5% against 3.5% in the US (Goldman Sachs).
quote_evidence: An index of the so-called "old economy" that removes AI-related names has gained just 5.5% since Jan. 1.
In other words, the AI investment boom didn't create the US advantage, but it is magnifying the US lead.
"The bloc has probably missed out on the AI investment boom," BNP Paribas economists James Egelhof and Andrew Husby wrote to clients.
why_it_matters_hint: Without AI-related companies, US shares have not beaten Europe this year, so the US lead rests on AI.
event_date: 11 Oct 2026 (publication date; market figures year to date)
notes: Original Yahoo Finance reporting. Yahoo discloses it is a portfolio company of funds managed by affiliates of Apollo Global Management, whose data it cites. The article does not define which companies count as AI-related.
